title: Jetha the orphan
hookLine: an orphaned boy selling boiled grams at Lahore comes to Goindval, serves, and marries Bibi Bhani

cards: A crowded market street in Lahore. Carts, dust, shouting. A small boy with a tray calls out to passersby: boiled grams, hot boiled grams.
Chickpeas, cooked and salted, a street snack that costs next to nothing. His name is Jetha. His parents have both died.
He's about seven, tradition says, selling snacks on the street to help keep himself alive. This Guru's story begins with almost nothing at all.

teach.b: Jetha went to live with his grandmother in Basarke, the very village Guru Amar Das came from.
So when pilgrims set out from there to see the Guru at Goindval, the young man went with them. And he stayed. He did what Amar Das had once done for Guru Angad: he served.
Tradition says he carried baskets of earth for the step-well, worked in the kitchen, went wherever a pair of hands was needed. No money, no family connections. Just his work.
The Guru's wife was looking for a husband for their daughter, Bibi Bhani. Tradition says she saw Jetha working and said: a young man like that. The Guru agreed.
The orphan who once sold grams on the street married the Guru's daughter. Bibi Bhani is honored in her own right, remembered for her devoted service to her father.
She would become the wife of one Guru, the mother of another, and the grandmother of a third. Jetha kept serving, for years.

teach.h: THE ORPHAN BECAME GURU RAM DAS.
teach.b: Eventually Guru Amar Das chose him as his successor, and he became the fourth Guru, Guru Ram Das.
Notice the baskets: Jetha carried earth for a step-well open to every caste, and the boy with nothing became family to the Guru.
Sikhs tell it to say that nobody's beginning is too small. The Gurus looked at who people could become, not where they started.

how: Sikhs honor Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, as the fourth Guru, and tell his orphaned childhood and years of service as a sign that the Gurus chose by devotion, not birth; Bibi Bhani is honored as a pillar of the early community.

o: the orphan boy who became Guru Ram Das
a pilgrim who led the trip to Goindval
Guru Amar Das's eldest son and heir

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: the name Jetha came to bear

s: the fourth Guru was born into a wealthy family
he was orphaned young and sold boiled grams on the street.
Bibi Bhani was wife, mother and grandmother of Gurus
wife of Guru Ram Das, mother of Guru Arjan, grandmother of Guru Hargobind.
Jetha came to Goindval with money and connections
he came with a group of pilgrims, and brought only his work.

games.q: you're the Guru's wife, looking for a husband for your daughter. you see a young orphan working hard on the step-well. what do you think?
o: he's got no family; not suitable.
he should work for us, not marry in.
games.why: tradition says she saw Jetha at work and wanted a husband like him. he married Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru.

practice: Picture Jetha with his tray, then picture someone you could hold a snack out to: a coworker, a kid, someone at the bus stop, a person on the street. A handful of nuts, a piece of fruit, a granola bar; small and simple.
For now, just see their face as they take it.

wordCard.voice: Jetha. The boy who sold boiled grams in Lahore, served at Goindval, married Bibi Bhani, and became Guru Ram Das.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Jetha, the childhood name of Guru Ram Das.

carryVoice: Your line: small beginnings. A tray of grams in Lahore, and then a Guru. Day fifty-four, done.
